prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Context: FAA NextGen aims to raise National Airspace System (NAS) capacity/efficiency. Adverse en route weather causes ~70% of US delays; a 2015 NASA survey ranked weather delays the costliest en route problem. System of interest: NASA Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3), integrated ground- and aircraft-based decision aids that continuously seek more efficient weather-avoidance routes, respond to weather changes and Traffic Management Initiatives (TMIs), and sustain en route/arrival metering. Subset: NASA Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR), cruise phase, using existing weather/airspace/traffic data and ATM automation; benefits: time, fuel, cost, emissions, workload savings. Current system: FAA traffic managers designate Flow Constrained Areas (FCA) and Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP), aka Playbook routes, 2-8 h ahead; these are static and conservative. Airline flight dispatchers file flight plans at least 45 min before push-back, revised per SWAP. Collaborative Trajectory Options Program (CTOP) allows multiple route options per flight plan but is strategic only. Air traffic controllers, dispatchers and flight crews manually request amendments at high workload; crews use flight management systems and on-board weather radar (limited range, no traffic view) and must consult controller/dispatch for alternate trajectories and coordinate with the controller on conflicts. Gap: no automation flags expired constraints or time/fuel-saving corrections. DWR description: ground-based, trajectory-based automation that continuously analyzes in-flight en route aircraft to find simple flight-plan route amendments saving significant flying time, accounting for convective weather, traffic conflicts, sector congestion, special use airspace and FAA routing restrictions. DWR sends route correction advisories (alerts) to the user (controller/dispatcher/flight crew), who can view/modify the route before requesting or issuing a route clearance; the DWR user interface must give strong warnings if a modified route's trial trajectory conflicts with forecast weather or traffic. DWR extends NASA's Direct-To tool (1998-2001); its integral Direct-To function identifies conflict-free, operationally acceptable direct routes, and any Direct-To route meeting the user-definable minimum wind-corrected time-savings threshold appears as a DWR advisory even without weather. Constraints are modeled as polygons, enabling non-weather obstacle use. No explicit modes yet.

New part:
U0050: DWR works by continuously and automatically analyzing in-flight aircraft operating within en route airspace above 10,000 ft to find opportunities for time- and fuel-saving corrections to weather avoidance routes, or simple wind-favorable direct to routes.
U0051: Route corrections are simple route changes like those typically used in today’s operations.
U0052: DWR analyzes and updates trajectories as new radar track and flight plan data are received [2].
U0053: DWR identifies flights that could save a user-defined minimum amount of time (default of five minutes) by short-cutting their current trajectory and returning to the flight plan trajectory via a downstream waypoint on their current flight plan route.
U0054: The DWR flight selection and route correction advisory logic are illustrated in Figures 1 and 2 and summarized as follows.
U0055: All flights at or above 10,000 ft are continuously and automatically analyzed to determine if a direct route trajectory from a Maneuver Start Point (MSP) to a default Return Capture Fix (RCF) could save the user-defined minimum time or more in wind-corrected flight time.
U0056: The MSP is programmable and currently defaults to a point 5 min downstream of present position or to the first point in the high altitude airspace.
U0057: The default RCF for any flight is intended to approximate an operationally acceptable direct route clearance given the location and routing of the flight, the local airspace, and arrival routing limits at the destination airport.
U0058: RCF selection is described in more detail below.
U0059: It is assumed that if a direct route to the RCF, the so-called reference direct route, can save 5 min or more, the flight is likely on some kind of weather avoidance route.
U0060: The reference direct route is then probed for weather and traffic conflicts.
U0061: If weather conflicts are detected, DWR automation inserts one or two auxiliary waypoints as needed in an attempt to identify a minimum delay route around the weather.
U0062: The MSP or any inserted waypoints may optionally be further adjusted automatically to achieve an integrated resolution to weather and traffic conflicts.
U0063: If a solution is found that can save the minimum wind-corrected flight time as defined by the user (5 min default), then a DWR route advisory is posted to an alert list on the user display.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
